---
title: "Data quality and completeness"
description: "How data quality affects BNR statistics and their interpretation."
---

BNR checks records and aggregate outputs before publication, but no health-information system is perfect. Public interpretation should account for completeness, timeliness, consistency and classification.

## Why this matters

A precise calculation can still give an incomplete picture if eligible events were missed or important fields were not recorded. Quality information helps readers judge what a statistic can support.

## Main dimensions of quality

| Dimension | Question to ask |
|---|---|
| **Coverage** | Are all intended sources, places and periods represented? |
| **Completeness** | Are the fields needed for the measure present? |
| **Validity** | Do values and dates satisfy the stated rules? |
| **Consistency** | Are definitions and coding applied similarly across records and time? |
| **Timeliness** | Has enough time passed for records and outcomes to be completed? |
| **Uniqueness** | Have duplicate representations of the same event been resolved? |

## Missing information and denominators

Some measures require more information than others. A case count may need an event type and date, while case fatality also needs a discharge outcome. A record can therefore be eligible for one statistic but not another.

Public percentages should state or make available the eligible denominator. Excluding records with missing information can affect comparability if missingness changes over time or differs between groups.

## Recent periods

Recent data are often less complete because abstraction, verification, discharge outcomes or death registration can take time. BNR may revise a recent period when later information becomes available.

## Quality checks and uncertainty

BNR checks required variables, logical date order, duplicates, unexpected values, output totals and disclosure-control results. Confidence intervals describe sampling or count uncertainty under a statistical model; they do not capture every form of missingness, misclassification or source coverage.

::: {.callout-tip title="Read limitations alongside results"}
A limitation does not make a statistic unusable. It defines the questions the statistic can answer safely and the comparisons that need caution.
:::

## What to remember

- Quality is specific to a measure and period.
- Missing values can change the analytical denominator.
- Recent figures may mature.
- Statistical precision and data completeness are different concepts.
